source.version: Undated manuscript headed 'Main Manuscript for', followed by Supporting Information. No publication date, journal citation, or arXiv version number is printed in the document; the filename's year is not treated as a confirmed manuscript date (PDF pp. 1, 17).
source.title_on_document: Designing Human and Generative AI Collaboration

supplement.where: Supporting Information occupies PDF pp. 17-57 (separately numbered SI pp. 1-41). PDF p. 17 also lists an MDAR Reproducibility Checklist as other supporting material; that checklist is not included in this PDF.
supplement.holds: Study design, recruitment, instructions, surveys, rating rubrics, regression specifications, Figure S1, and Tables S1-S12. Table S4 (PDF p. 48) supplies coefficients and standard errors for originality, interestingness, writing quality, and coherence; Table S7 (PDF p. 51) supplies overall-quality coefficients and standard errors. Tables S8-S9 (PDF pp. 52-53) give skill-heterogeneity analyses. No separate table or stated interval/test procedure for content-diversity results was found.

paper_design_summary: University students in an elective course on emerging technologies wrote a story without AI on Day 1 and a new story with ChatGPT 3.5 on Day 2, when they were randomly assigned among Human Confirmation, Human Creativity, and Copilot collaboration modes (PDF pp. 4, 18-20). Four human evaluators rated each story, and computed measures assessed genres per story and similarity across writers (PDF pp. 6-7, 16, 19-23). The between-mode comparisons are randomized coursework comparisons; the no-AI versus AI comparisons follow a fixed day order and are not randomized AI-access contrasts.

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual students were randomly assigned to one of three Day 2 AI collaboration modes. Everyone first wrote without AI on Day 1; AI availability/order itself was not randomized. This is coded field_rct because the experiment used an exercise within an elective course (PDF pp. 4, 18).
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to one of three AI collaboration models:
assignment.locator: PDF p. 4, Theoretical Background and Experimental Design; PDF p. 20 (SI p. 4), Figure S1.

arms.name: Human Confirmation
arms.description: Day 2, T1 (Group B in instructions): ChatGPT performs ideation, outlining, drafting, and editing; students prompt, accept/reject, or request regeneration, and may not introduce their own ideas (PDF pp. 4, 18, 26-27).

arms.name: Human Creativity
arms.description: Day 2, T2 (Group A in instructions): students ideate and outline without AI; ChatGPT drafts and edits. During production students prompt and accept/reject output but may not introduce additional ideas or directly write/edit (PDF pp. 4, 18-19, 28-29).

arms.name: Copilot
arms.description: Day 2, T3 (Group C in instructions): students and ChatGPT collaborate iteratively at every stage; students may provide ideas, write, edit, and request suggestions or feedback (PDF pp. 4, 19, 30-31). This is the unrestricted/default chatbot configuration for coding ai_design contrasts.

arms.name: Writing without AI (Day 1)
arms.description: All students first write a story manually without AI. This is the shared, fixed-order baseline, not a separately randomized arm or an after-AI assessment (PDF pp. 4, 19-20, 24-25).

participants.exclusions: PDF p. 18 states that all submitted stories were included, including those taking longer than the recommended 105 minutes (7 participants on Day 1 and 3 on Day 2). The paper reports 285 successfully participating students but does not print a distinct analyzed-person total, per-arm people counts, or a participant flow reconciling the missing records. Table 1 (PDF p. 11) has 280 initial-survey/DAT records; PDF p. 21 has 549 stories (278 Day 1, 271 Day 2) and 2,196 ratings. Table 1 also reports 508 exit-survey observations across days and 248 Day 2 AI-support survey records; PDF p. 42 reports reflective feedback from 197 participants. These are different outcome samples; none is relabeled as an overall analyzed-person count. No intention-to-treat claim is made.
participants.who: Students in an elective course on emerging technologies, participating through a classroom exercise with course-credit incentives. The paper reports 285 participants. Four ratings per story came from two fellow participants and two external student research assistants; nine external evaluators were recruited, and are not added to the writer sample (PDF pp. 18-19).
participants.quote: A total of 285 students successfully participated in the experiment.
participants.locator: PDF p. 18 (SI p. 2), A.1 Participants and Participant Recruitment; PDF p. 21 (SI p. 5), A.2 Data and Variables; PDF p. 11, Table 1.

ai_tool.how_used: Students used ChatGPT after prompt-engineering training, with permissions determined by the assigned mode; Copilot allowed free collaboration throughout, while Human Confirmation and Human Creativity restricted human contributions as described in the arms (PDF pp. 4, 18-19, 26-31). GPT-4o was used separately to classify genres (PDF p. 6), and OpenAI text-embedding-3-large to measure semantic similarity (PDF p. 16); these were measurement tools, not the assigned writing assistant.

task.description: Produce a new 1,000-word short story on each of two study days, with any genre allowed. The process comprised ideation, outlining, drafting, and editing, supported by instruction in a seven-sequence narrative structure (PDF pp. 4, 24-33).
task.duration: Main text specifies a 105-minute writing session each day (PDF p. 4); SI recruitment and Figure S1 also specify 105 minutes, with recruitment additionally specifying 15-minute surveys (PDF pp. 18, 20). SI task descriptions instead specify 75 minutes each day (PDF p. 19). The discrepancy is unresolved; the calendar interval between days is not stated.

outcomes.name: Overall story quality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Each story received four 1-7 ratings from two fellow participants and two external student research assistants, blinded to writer identity and collaboration condition (PDF pp. 19, 21, 41). Primary between-mode regressions use individual evaluations, with DAT, writing experience, writing ability, and English proficiency controls (PDF pp. 23, 44, 48, 51). The paper does not state participant/story clustering or evaluator effects. n_units = 2,196 is the reported total number of evaluations for this metric across both days and all arms (PDF pp. 11, 21), not a Day 2 contrast-specific sample size; regression-specific Ns are unreported. Day 1 comparisons are fixed-order before_after comparisons. Holistic rubric asks whether the story conveys its main ideas creatively, interestingly, coherently, and with good writing (PDF pp. 21, 41). Overall mean 4.91, SD 1.35 across all ratings (PDF p. 11, Table 1); this is not an arm-specific or participant-level SD. Table S7 reports models with and without covariates as robustness variants of this outcome. Skill-heterogeneity analyses are not additional outcomes: Table S8 (PDF p. 52) instead averages ratings to the participant/story level and regresses Day 2 quality on Day 1 quality; adjusted slopes are Human Confirmation 0.0864 (SE 0.114), Human Creativity 0.2442** (SE 0.093), and Copilot 0.2069** (SE 0.095), with ** p < 0.05. Table S9 (PDF p. 53) uses evaluation-level ratings and reports adjusted DAT coefficients 0.0139** (SE 0.006) on Day 1 and -0.0005 (SE 0.006) on Day 2; ** p < 0.05. Figure 2E (PDF p. 13) further displays quality by baseline DAT subgroup. Table S5 (PDF p. 49) models associations of the other four ratings with overall quality, rather than an AI treatment contrast.

contrasts.reported: The main text states that overall story quality did not differ significantly between Human Creativity and Copilot on Day 2. No exact pairwise estimate, standard error, or p-value for this contrast is printed; it has not been calculated by subtracting the coefficients against Human Confirmation.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5, Writing Quality; PDF p. 51, Table S7.

contrasts.reported: Table S7 prints the reverse orientation, Copilot minus Human Confirmation: Day 2 adjusted coefficient 0.3158*** (SE 0.105); without covariates 0.2628** (SE 0.104). Here the treatment is Human Confirmation, so the quality direction is lower. Main text: difference = 0.32, P < 0.01. Table significance key: ** p < 0.05, *** p < 0.01.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 51 (SI p. 35), Table S7; PDF p. 5, Writing Quality.

contrasts.reported: Human Creativity minus Human Confirmation on Day 2: adjusted coefficient 0.3376*** (SE 0.106); without covariates 0.2780*** (SE 0.103). Main text: difference = 0.34, P < 0.01. Table significance key: *** p < 0.01.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 51 (SI p. 35), Table S7; PDF p. 5, Writing Quality.

outcomes.name: Semantic similarity between different writers' stories
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity of each completed story embedding to the mean embedding of the other stories in its condition; measured using OpenAI text-embedding-3-large (PDF p. 16). Figure 4C shows kernel-density distributions, means, and 95% CIs. n_units = 549 is the full story corpus across both days (PDF p. 21); arm-specific output counts and analysis-specific Ns are not printed. The scored outputs are final stories written with the assigned AI access; Human Creativity's initial unaided ideation does not make this an after_ai outcome.

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity between each story's text embedding and the average embedding of other stories in the same condition.
diversity_detail.computed_over: One similarity value for each story, compared with the mean embedding of all other stories in its condition. Conditions are the three Day 2 collaboration modes and pooled Day 1 writing without AI; these are not all pairwise comparisons (PDF pp. 6-7, 16).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Condition means and 95% confidence intervals are printed, but the interval calculation and significance-test procedure are not stated. No dependence correction, bootstrap, permutation method, or independent-unit standard error is identified (PDF pp. 6-7, 15-16).
diversity_detail.notes: Higher raw similarity means less diversity. The contrast directions reverse this orientation, while every reported number remains in the paper's original similarity units. No standardized effect or difference was calculated. Before_after comparisons do not isolate AI access from day/order effects.

outcomes.name: Genre similarity between different writers' stories
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: GPT-4o classified each story into one or more of nine literary-fiction genres (PDF p. 6). Cosine similarity then compares a story's nine binary genre indicators with the mean genre vector of other stories in its condition (PDF p. 16). category_count is the closest vocabulary category for this classification-based measure; these genre indicators are not text embeddings. Figure 4B shows density plots and condition means with 95% CIs. n_units = 549 is the full story corpus, not a count of independent pairs or a contrast-specific N (PDF p. 21).

contrasts.reported: Human Creativity: mean = 0.533, 95% CI = [0.526, 0.539]; Copilot: mean = 0.527, 95% CI = [0.521, 0.534]. Raw values are similarity, so the diversity direction is reversed. No exact pairwise test for Human Creativity versus Copilot is printed; the paper does not claim a clear difference between them.

eligibility.reason: Core eligibility is supported by randomized assignment to different generative-AI configurations, not randomized AI versus no-AI access (PDF p. 4; Figure S1, PDF p. 20). The study reports 285 successfully participating students and includes all submitted stories; its initial participant-characteristic analysis includes 280 people, and the protocol calls for one story per student on each day, with 271 Day 2 stories evaluated, clearly supporting the at-least-50 criterion (PDF pp. 11, 18-21). Exact unique writer counts in each outcome regression and each arm remain unreported, so the analyzed-person fields are null. Human ratings assess originality and holistic story quality, and computed similarities compare different writers' stories (PDF pp. 4, 6-7, 16, 41). Only the ai_design contrasts satisfy the random-assignment criterion; before_after contrasts do not. No unassisted post-AI outcome was measured.

one_line_finding: Human Creativity and Copilot exceeded Human Confirmation in overall story quality by 0.3376 (SE 0.106) and 0.3158 (SE 0.105), respectively (both p < 0.01; PDF p. 51, Table S7), while semantic similarity was 0.710, 0.743, and 0.779, respectively (PDF p. 7).
open_questions: What were the numbers of people assigned and analyzed in each arm and regression, and how do the reported 285 participants, 280 initial-survey records, and 278/271 daily story counts reconcile? (PDF pp. 11, 18, 21.)

Do the rating-level standard errors in Tables S4 and S7 account for repeated evaluations of the same participant/story or shared evaluators? The printed specification does not state clustering or random effects (PDF p. 23).

How were confidence intervals and significance tests for genre and semantic similarity computed, including dependence induced by each story's comparison to the other stories in its condition? The PDF does not specify this (PDF pp. 6-7, 15-16).
Was the task limit 105 minutes, as stated in the main text, recruitment section, and Figure S1, or 75 minutes, as stated in the SI day-specific task descriptions? (PDF pp. 4, 18-20.)
What manuscript date/version does this saved PDF represent? The printed document does not identify a date, journal version, or arXiv revision.
notes: Extracted by screener B on 2026-10-09. Locators use physical PDF pages; Supporting Information starts at PDF p. 17 and has its own page numbers. The complete markdown conversion and all PDF pages were covered, including tables, figures, instructions, surveys, and SI references; PDF text/table extraction and in-memory page images resolved omitted figures and scrambled markdown tables. No effect sizes, confidence limits, arm differences, or sample sizes were computed. There is one classroom experiment; baseline-skill subgroup analyses are not additional studies. The nine coded output outcomes are overall quality, originality, interestingness, writing quality, coherence, semantic similarity, genre similarity, genres per story, and genre composition. Self-reported completion time (total and four stages), process satisfaction, process flexibility, process effectiveness, intent to reuse, AI satisfaction, AI effectiveness, perceived AI contribution, and the positive/negative reflective-feedback topic frequencies are outside the scored-output outcome scope (PDF pp. 12, 14, 42-47, 50, 54-56). Baseline DAT is a participant characteristic, not an AI-assistance outcome. The discussion additionally describes twenty ChatGPT 3.5 DAT tests (mean 85.7, range 82-88) against participants' baseline performance (mean 82.2, range 65-95; PDF p. 8); this ancillary model benchmark is retained here, not counted as another human-assistance study or an after_ai effect. Table 1 reports the human DAT mean more precisely as 82.28 (SD 7.13; n = 280; PDF p. 11). Quality subgroup/inequality and covariate-robustness analyses are described under the overall-quality measure, not counted as separate outcomes. No single primary outcome or preregistration is explicitly designated; primary fields therefore remain not_stated. Overall quality is coded overall_creativity because its rubric explicitly integrates creativity, interestingness, writing, and coherence (PDF pp. 21, 41); originality remains a separate novelty outcome. Genre breadth within one story is coded flexibility, while the two between-writer similarity measures and condition-level genre distributions are coded diversity. For similarity, contrast direction is normalized so higher means more diversity; raw similarity statistics are preserved unchanged. In ai_design comparisons, Copilot serves as the default configuration; when a table prints the reverse subtraction, reported explicitly states its original orientation without calculating a reversed coefficient. The data and code URLs are printed on PDF p. 9; the repository was not used to derive additional quantities.
